items.basis: The proposed mechanism fails to address the fundamental physics of peristaltic pump occlusion, which by design concentrates force on a single tube line at any given moment. The evidence [doi:10.1016/s0262-1762(03)00715-6] explicitly states that peristaltic pumps operate by sequentially compressing tubing sections, making distributed stress physically impossible with this pump type.

The candidate ignores the boundary condition of limited space in a "compact peristaltic dosing pump head," making implementation of multiple pressure transducers and adaptive control systems impossible within the existing form factor. The evidence [doi:10.1016/s0262-1762(04)00163-4] emphasizes the compact nature of these devices as a key design constraint.

The evidence [doi:10.32786/2071-9485-2018-03-324-329] demonstrates that rotary peristaltic pump performance is optimized through fixed occlusion forces, directly contradicting the candidate's proposed adaptive pressure control approach which would introduce unnecessary complexity and potential for dosing inaccuracy.

The candidate fails to explain how adaptive pressure control maintains "precise dosing accuracy" when the baseline already achieves acceptable precision for water-quality analysis. The evidence [doi:10.52338/jows.2026.5561] shows that peristaltic pumps for water applications operate effectively with standard fixed occlusion forces.

The proposed adaptive control system requires real-time feedback across all tubing lines simultaneously, which is technically impossible in a peristaltic pump where only one tube is occluded at a time. The evidence [doi:10.1186/s13244-024-01750-4] confirms that pressure feedback systems in medical applications require continuous pressure monitoring, which cannot be achieved with sequential occlusion.

The testable prediction fails to account for the dynamic nature of tubing fatigue, which occurs over time and cycles rather than being measurable as a static "stress distribution pattern." The evidence [doi:10.1016/s0262-1762(03)00715-6] indicates that tubing failure is a time-dependent fatigue process that cannot be adequately assessed through static measurements alone.
